all-purpose thread.d: Medium-weight polyester thread that works for most sewing. Use the same thread on top and in the bobbin.

backstitch.d: By machine: a few stitches sewn in reverse at the start and end of a seam to lock it. By hand: a strong stitch where each stitch goes back to meet the last one.

bar tack.d: A short, dense zigzag sewn in one spot to make it strong, like the ends of a buttonhole or the corners of a pocket.

baste.d: To sew long, temporary stitches that hold pieces in place until the real seam is sewn. Basting is easy to pull out.

bias.d: The 45° diagonal across woven fabric. It stretches much more than the grain, which is why bias-cut garments drape and bias strips bend around curves.

bias strip.d: A strip of fabric cut at 45° to the grain, so it stretches a little and bends smoothly around curves.

bias tape.d: Bias strips pressed so the raw edges are hidden. Single-fold has both edges pressed to the middle. Double-fold is folded in half again, and its strip is cut 4 times the finished width.

binding.d: A strip, usually cut on the bias, that wraps around a raw edge and shows on both sides, finishing it.

blend.d: A fabric made of two or more fibers, like polyester-cotton. The label lists the percent of each. Care for it the way its fussiest fiber needs.

dia.care: Machine wash warm, tumble dry low

blend sizes.d: To draw a smooth cutting line from one size to another on a multi-size pattern, for example a size 12 waist to a size 16 hip.

blind hem.d: A hem stitched so only tiny dots show on the right side. Sewn by hand, or with a machine's blind hem stitch, which sews a few straight stitches and then a small bite into the fold.

bobbin.d: The small spool of thread that sits under the needle plate. Its thread locks with the top thread to form each stitch.

bodice.d: The part of a garment from the shoulders to the waist.

bolt.d: The roll or folded board that fabric is wrapped on in a shop. The label on its end lists the fiber, the width, and the care.

boxed corner.d: A corner flattened into a triangle and stitched straight across, giving a bag or pouch a flat bottom.

burn test.d: Safely burning a tiny strip of fabric to tell its fiber family by the flame, the smell, and what's left: soft ash (plant), crumbly black ash (animal), or a hard bead (synthetic).

buttonhole.d: A finished slit for a button: two narrow zigzag sides and a bar tack at each end. Its length is the button's width plus its thickness.

canvas.d: A sturdy, tightly woven cotton fabric used for bags, aprons, and outerwear. Duck is a similar, smoother fabric.

care label.d: The tag in a garment that shows how to wash, bleach, dry, iron, and dry clean it, usually with small symbols.

casing.d: A folded and stitched tunnel that holds elastic or a drawstring.

center back.d: The line down the exact middle of a garment's back, often written CB. A center back seam joins two back pieces there.

center front.d: The line down the exact middle of a garment's front. On patterns it's often written CF, and it's where buttons sit.

centered zipper.d: A zipper set under a seam so the two folded edges meet over the teeth, with a line of stitching on each side.

clapper.d: A smooth block of hardwood held down on a spot right after steaming it. It traps the heat and sets a crisp, flat edge.

clip.d: A small straight snip into a seam allowance, stopping just short of the stitching. Clips let inward curves and corners lie flat.

collar.d: The piece that finishes and frames the neckline. On a shirt, it folds over a band called the collar stand.

collar stand.d: The band a shirt collar is sewn onto. It stands up around the neck and holds the top button.

colorfast.d: Dye that doesn't run or rub off when it's wet. Test dark and bright fabrics before you wash them with anything else.

cotton.d: A plant fiber from the fluffy pods around cotton seeds. Breathable, washable, strong, and easy to sew and press. It wrinkles and can shrink.

crosswise grain.d: The direction from one selvedge to the other, across the fabric. It has a little more give than the lengthwise grain.

crotch seam.d: The curved seam that runs from the front waist, between the legs, to the back waist. It takes a lot of strain, so it's often stitched twice in the curve.

cuff.d: A band that finishes the end of a sleeve or pant leg.

cutting layout.d: A map on the instruction sheet showing how to fold the fabric and place each piece, for a given view, width, and size.

cutting line.d: The outer line of a pattern piece. You cut on it. The stitching line is one seam allowance inside it.

dart.d: A wedge of fabric folded and stitched to a point, so flat fabric curves around the body, like at the bust or waist.

design ease.d: Extra room a designer adds on top of wearing ease to create a style, like a relaxed shirt or roomy pajama pants.

dot.d: A round mark on a pattern piece showing where to start or stop stitching, turn, gather, or match two pieces.

double-fold hem.d: A hem folded up twice so the raw edge is hidden inside, then stitched close to the inner fold.

drape.d: How a fabric hangs and falls into folds. Fluid fabrics fall close, in many soft folds. Stiff fabrics stand away in a few wide ones.

ease.d: The extra room a garment has beyond your body measurements. It's made of wearing ease (room to move) plus design ease (room for the style).

easing.d: Working a slightly longer edge into a shorter one smoothly, with no tucks, by spreading the extra length evenly. A long stitch you can pull up helps.

edgestitch.d: A line of stitching very close to an edge or fold, usually about 1/8 in (3 mm) away. It holds layers flat and looks crisp.

elastic.d: A stretchy band, usually sold by width. In a casing it gathers a waist so it pulls on and holds itself up. Firm, flat elastic about 1 in (2.5 cm) wide suits most pajama waists.

fabric weight.d: How heavy a fabric is for its size, in ounces per square yard (oz/yd²) or grams per square meter (g/m²). Roughly: light is under 4 oz/yd² (135 g/m²), medium is 4 to 8 oz/yd² (135 to 270 g/m²), and heavy is more.

facing.d: A shaped piece that copies an edge, like a neckline, and is sewn on and turned to the inside to finish it neatly.

feed dogs.d: The little metal teeth under the presser foot that move the fabric along as you sew.

felting.d: When heat, soap, and rubbing make wool's tiny scales lock together, so the fabric shrinks and thickens for good.

fiber.d: A single hair-thin strand, like one wisp of cotton fluff. Fibers are twisted into yarn, and yarn becomes fabric. The fiber decides a lot about how a fabric feels, washes, and presses.

finished measurements.d: The measurements of the sewn garment itself, not of the body. Finished minus body measurement tells you how much ease a pattern has.

flat-felled seam.d: A strong seam with both raw edges folded inside and stitched flat, so two rows of stitching show. Common on shirts and jeans.

float.d: A stretch of thread that passes over several threads at once instead of going over and under each one. Long floats make satin shiny, and easier to snag.

fray.d: When threads unravel from a cut edge of woven fabric. Finishing the edges stops it.

french seam.d: A seam sewn twice: first wrong sides together, then right sides together, so the raw edges are sealed inside. The two passes add up to the usual seam allowance.

fusible.d: Having glue on one side that melts and sticks when pressed with an iron, like fusible interfacing.

gathers.d: Small, soft folds made by pulling up long stitches, so a long edge fits onto a shorter one. Usually 1.5 to 2 times the length of the edge they're sewn to.

grade.d: Trimming the layers of a seam allowance to different widths so the edge isn't bulky. The layer that ends up nearest the outside stays widest.

grain.d: The direction the threads run in a woven fabric. Lengthwise grain runs parallel to the selvedge; crosswise grain runs across.

grainline.d: The long arrow on a pattern piece. Lay it parallel to the selvedge so the piece is cut on grain.

hand.d: How a fabric feels to touch: soft or crisp, smooth or textured, cool or warm, slippery or grippy, and springy or limp.

handwheel.d: The wheel on the right side of the machine that moves the needle by hand. Always turn the top of it toward you.

hem.d: The finished bottom edge of a garment or item, usually folded up and stitched.

hem allowance.d: The extra fabric below the finished length that folds up to make the hem. Your pattern says how much.

high bust.d: A measurement taken high under the arms, above the fullest part of the chest. If your full bust is 2 in (5 cm) or more bigger, use your high bust to pick a top size.

hook and eye.d: A small metal fastener sewn on by hand, often just above a zipper at the waist.

in-seam pocket.d: A pocket hidden in a side seam, with its bag inside the garment.

inseam.d: The seam along the inside of each pant leg, from the hem to the crotch. It's also the name of the inside leg measurement.

instruction sheet.d: The paper inside a pattern with the piece list, cutting layouts, a shading key, abbreviations, and numbered sewing steps.

interfacing.d: An extra layer on the wrong side of fabric that makes it firmer. It hides inside collars, cuffs, waistbands, plackets, and facings. It can be fusible (irons on) or sew-in.

invisible zipper.d: A zipper whose coil hides inside the seam, so only the pull shows. It's sewn in before the seam, with a special foot.

knit.d: Fabric made of rows of interlocking loops, like a t-shirt or sweater. Knits stretch.

ladder stitch.d: A hand stitch that closes a gap between two folded edges. The stitches cross straight between the folds and disappear when pulled tight.

lapped zipper.d: A zipper hidden under a flap, with one line of stitching showing on the flap side.

lengthen/shorten line.d: A pair of parallel lines across a pattern piece. Spread the piece here to add length, or fold it to take length away.

lengthwise grain.d: The direction parallel to the selvedge. It's the strongest direction and barely stretches. Most pattern pieces follow it.

linen.d: A plant fiber from the stems of the flax plant. Strong, cool, and crisp. It wrinkles easily, frays more than cotton, and softens with washing.

lining.d: A second layer inside a bag or garment that hides the seams and raw edges and makes it feel nicer.

multi-size pattern.d: A pattern with several sizes printed on each piece, nested inside each other, each with its own line style.

nap.d: A fabric surface with a direction, like velvet, corduroy, or faux fur. It looks lighter or darker depending on which way it points, so every piece is cut the same way up.

needle plate.d: The metal plate under the presser foot, with a hole for the needle and guide lines for seam allowances.

needle size.d: Machine needles are sized with two numbers, like 80/12. The bigger the number, the thicker the needle.

nonwoven.d: Fabric made by pressing or bonding fibers into a sheet, with no threads or loops. Felt and most interfacing are nonwovens. It has no grain and doesn't fray.

notch.d: A small triangle on a pattern's cutting line that matches a notch on another piece. One notch usually marks a front edge, two a back edge. (Cutting V shapes into a curve is a different job: see 'notch a curve.')

notch a curve.d: Cutting little V shapes out of the seam allowance on an outward curve, so it lies flat when turned. (On patterns, a notch is also a small mark used to match pieces: you'll meet that in level 4.)

notions.d: Everything a project needs besides the fabric: thread, elastic, buttons, zippers, interfacing, and so on. The envelope back lists them.

nylon.d: A synthetic fiber made from oil. Very strong, smooth, and a little stretchy. Used in raincoats, bags, swimsuits, and linings. It melts under a hot iron.

one-way design.d: A print whose motifs all face one direction, like trees standing up. Every pattern piece has to be cut the same way up.

one-way print.d: A print whose motifs only look right one way up, like trees, animals, or words. Cut it with a with-nap layout.

patch pocket.d: A pocket sewn on top of a garment, like on a shirt front.

pattern.d: A set of paper templates, one for each piece of a garment, plus instructions for sewing it. You lay the pieces on fabric and cut around them.

pattern envelope.d: The envelope a store pattern comes in. The front shows the design and its views. The back lists fabrics, notions, sizes, yardage, and finished measurements.

pattern repeat.d: How far along the fabric you go before a print starts over. Bigger repeats take more fabric to match.

pattern weights.d: Small heavy objects that hold a pattern flat on fabric or tracing paper instead of pins. Cans, big washers, and smooth stones work too.

pilling.d: Tiny balls of fuzz that form where fabric rubs, like under the arms. Common on polyester and on soft, loosely spun fabrics.

pinking shears.d: Scissors with zigzag blades. The zigzag edge frays less than a straight cut.

pivot.d: Turning the fabric around the needle (needle down, foot up) to sew a sharp corner.

place on fold.d: A bracket with arrows on a pattern piece. Put that edge exactly on the folded edge of the fabric and don't cut it, so the piece opens out twice as wide with no seam.

placket.d: A finished opening in a garment, like the doubled strip that holds the buttons on a shirt front.

plain weave.d: The simplest weave: each thread goes over one and under one. Firm, crisp, and strong. Poplin, lawn, and canvas are plain weaves.

pleat.d: A fold of fabric pressed or stitched in place to control fullness.

pocket bag.d: The inside part of a pocket, the bit that holds your things.

point turner.d: A smooth, pointed tool for gently pushing out corners, like collar points, after turning.

polyester.d: A synthetic fiber made from oil. Strong, quick-drying, and wrinkle resistant, and it barely shrinks. It breathes less than natural fibers and melts under a hot iron.

press.d: Lifting the iron, setting it down, and holding it, instead of sliding it. Pressing shapes and flattens without stretching.

press open.d: Spreading the two seam allowances apart and pressing them flat on either side of the seam.

presser foot.d: The metal foot that holds the fabric flat against the feed dogs while you sew. Lower it before every seam.

pressing cloth.d: A piece of plain cotton or organza laid between the iron and your fabric to prevent shine and scorching.

pressing ham.d: A firm, rounded cushion for pressing curved parts like darts and sleeve tops, so they keep their shape.

prewash.d: Washing and drying fabric before cutting, the same way you'll wash the finished item, so it shrinks before you sew it.

print scale.d: How big the motifs in a print are. Small prints read as texture, and large ones read as separate shapes.

quilting cotton.d: A medium-weight, plain-woven cotton. Stable, easy to sew and press: the best fabric to learn on.

raw edge.d: A cut edge of fabric that isn't finished yet, so it can fray.

rayon.d: A fiber made in factories from wood pulp. Soft, cool, and very drapey. It's weak when wet and can shrink, so wash it gently.
rayon.also: viscose; close cousins are modal and lyocell

right side.d: The front of the fabric, meant to show on the outside. In Notch diagrams it's colored with dots.

right sides together.d: Placing two pieces face to face, pretty sides touching, before sewing. The seam ends up on the inside.

rotary cutter.d: A round blade on a handle, rolled along a ruler on a cutting mat. Great for straight cuts.

running stitch.d: The simplest hand stitch: in and out along a line. Used for basting and gathering.

satin weave.d: A weave with long floats on the surface, which makes a smooth, shiny, slippery face. In cotton it's called sateen.

seam.d: The line of stitching that joins two pieces of fabric.

seam allowance.d: The distance between the cut edge and the stitching line. Notch always uses 5/8 in (1.5 cm), like most store patterns.

seam gauge.d: A short ruler with a sliding marker, for measuring and repeating small distances like hems.

seam ripper.d: A small tool with a sharp hook for cutting and removing stitches.

seam sealant.d: A clear liquid that dries soft and stops cut threads from fraying. Handy on buttonhole slits.

selvedge.d: The tightly woven, finished edge along both long sides of fabric. It doesn't fray.

serger.d: A machine that sews a seam, trims the edge, and wraps it in thread all at once. Nice to have, never required.

shank.d: The short stem under a button, made of wrapped thread or built into the button. It gives the buttonhole layer room to sit.

shrinkage.d: How much smaller a fabric gets when it's washed and dried, as a percent. Cotton and linen often shrink 3% to 5% the first time.

side seam.d: The seam that runs down each side of a garment, under the arm or along the hip.

silhouette.d: A garment's outline, the shape you'd see in its shadow: A-line, straight, full, and so on. Fabric drape changes it a lot.

silk.d: An animal fiber from the cocoon a silkworm spins. Smooth, shiny, drapey, and strong for its weight. Often slippery to sew.

size chart.d: The table of body measurements for each pattern size. You pick your size by comparing your own measurements with it. Pattern sizes are not shop sizes.

slip stitch.d: A nearly invisible hand stitch for hems: a tiny catch in the main fabric, then a slide inside the fold.

snip.d: A tiny cut, 1/8 to 1/4 in (3 to 6 mm), into the seam allowance to mark a notch, a fold line's end, or a center point.

spandex.d: A very stretchy synthetic fiber. A few percent mixed into cotton or polyester gives a fabric stretch, and helps it spring back.

spool pin.d: The post on top of the machine that holds your spool of thread.

staystitch.d: A line of regular stitching through one layer, just inside the seam allowance, that keeps a curved or slanted edge from stretching. Sew it soon after cutting, from the wide end toward the narrow end.

stitch in the ditch.d: Stitching from the right side right in the groove of a seam, so it hides there. It holds a facing, casing, or waistband in place.

stitch length.d: How long each stitch is, in millimeters. 2.5 mm is the everyday length for seams.

stitching line.d: Where the seam is sewn, one seam allowance in from the cutting line. Most store patterns don't print it.

swatch.d: A small sample piece of fabric, kept to look at, test, and compare.

tailor's chalk.d: Flat chalk for marking fabric. It brushes off.

tailor's tack.d: A loose loop of doubled thread stitched through a mark and both fabric layers, then snipped between the layers so each keeps a tuft. Good for fabrics chalk won't show on.

take-up lever.d: The arm that moves up and down above the needle. It pulls each stitch snug, and the thread must pass through it.

technical flat.d: A line drawing of a garment laid flat, front and back, showing every seam, dart, and line of stitching. Solid lines are seams and edges; dashed lines are stitching you can see.

tension.d: How tightly the threads are held as stitches form. Balanced tension means the threads lock inside the fabric.

topstitch.d: Stitching on the right side that shows, used to hold layers flat and as decoration. Usually 1/4 in (6 mm) or so from an edge or seam.

trace.d: To copy your size and all its marks onto new paper, so the original pattern stays whole with every size.

tracing paper.d: Paper with one colored side, waxy or chalky. Put the colored side against the fabric's wrong side and roll a tracing wheel over the pattern to copy lines.

tracing wheel.d: A small toothed wheel on a handle. Rolled along a pattern's lines over tracing paper, it leaves dotted lines on the fabric.

trim.d: Cutting away extra seam allowance, like snipping the point off a corner so it turns out sharp.

true.d: To redraw an edge smoothly after changing a pattern, so there are no steps or jogs and the matching seams are the same length.

twill.d: A weave where each thread goes over two or more and under one or more, starting one step over on each row. That makes diagonal lines. Denim and gabardine are twills.

understitch.d: Stitching through a facing and both seam allowances, close to the seam, so the facing rolls to the inside and stays hidden.

universal needle.d: The everyday machine needle, with a slightly rounded point that works on most wovens and many knits.

view.d: One version of the design inside a pattern, named with a letter: view A, view B, and so on. Views share some pieces and differ in details like length, sleeves, or pockets.

warp.d: The lengthwise threads in a woven fabric, held tight on the loom. They run parallel to the selvedge, along the lengthwise grain.

wearing ease.d: The least extra room a woven garment needs so you can move, sit, and breathe: roughly 2 in (5 cm) at the hip, 2 to 3 in (5 to 7.5 cm) at the bust, and 1 in (2.5 cm) at the waist.

weft.d: The crosswise threads in a woven fabric, passed over and under the warp from one selvedge to the other.

with nap.d: A layout or yardage where every pattern piece points the same way. Use it for napped fabrics, one-way prints, and shiny fabrics. 'Without nap' layouts can turn pieces head to toe.

wool.d: An animal fiber, usually sheep's fleece. Warm, springy, and easy to shape with steam. Hot water and rubbing make it felt and shrink.

woven.d: Fabric made of threads crossing over and under each other at right angles. Wovens don't stretch much, except on the bias.

wrong side.d: The back of the fabric, meant to face the inside. In Notch diagrams it's striped.

yardage.d: How much fabric a project needs, measured in yards (or meters). It depends on the fabric's width.

yardage chart.d: The table on a pattern envelope that says how much fabric to buy. Find your view, your fabric's width, and your size: the amount is where they meet.

yarn.d: Fibers twisted together into one long strand. Woven and knit fabrics are both made from yarn.

yoke.d: A fitted piece across the shoulders (on shirts) or hips (on skirts and jeans) that other pieces hang from.

zigzag stitch.d: A side-to-side machine stitch. Used to finish raw edges and, later, for stretchy fabrics.

zipper foot.d: A narrow presser foot that lets the needle sew right next to zipper teeth.
